Suppose:\n   294\t\n   295\t- Draw 1 (from “Mixed”) → C → so true C = bag labeled “Mixed”\n   296\t- Draw 2 (from “Chocolates”) → M\n   297\t\n   298\tNow possibilities:\n   299\t\n   300\t**Possibility 1**: “Chocolates” bag = pure M  \n   301\t→ Then Mixed bag is either C+G or M+G  \n   302\tBut C+G doesn’t contain M, M+G does.\n   303\t\n   304\t**Possibility 2**: “Chocolates” bag = Mixed = C+M  \n   305\t→ Then pure M must be in either “Mints” or “Gum” bag.\n   306\t\n   307\tBut bag labeled “Mints” can’t be M, so pure M would have to be in bag labeled “Gum”.\n   308\t\n   309\tSimilarly, pure G would be in bag labeled “Mints”.\n   310\t\n   311\tNow, check consistency:\n   312\t\n   313\t- In Possibility 1 (Chocolates = pure M):\n   314\t  - Pure M = “Chocolates”\n   315\t  - Pure C = “Mixed”\n   316\t  - Remaining bags: “Mints” and “Gum” → must be G and Mixed\n   317\t  - “Mints” ≠ M → OK to be G or Mixed\n   318\t  - “Gum” ≠ G → OK to be M (but M already used) or Mixed → so “Gum” must be Mixed\n   319\t  - Then “Mints” = G\n   320\t\n   321\t  So Mixed = “Gum”\n   322\t\n   323\t- In Possibility 2 (Chocolates = Mixed = C+M):\n   324\t  - Pure C = “Mixed”\n   325\t  - Mixed = “Chocolates”\n   326\t  - Remaining: “Mints” and “Gum” → must be pure M and pure G\n   327\t  - “Mints” ≠ M → so must be G\n   328\t  - “Gum” ≠ G → so must be M\n   329\t\n   330\tBoth scenarios are logically consistent with all constraints and the two observations.\n   331\t\n   332\tAnd they lead to **different labelings**:\n   333\t\n   334\t- In P1: “Gum” is Mixed\n   335\t- In P2: “Chocolates” is Mixed\n   336\t\n   337\tSo with only two draws (C from “Mixed”, M from “Chocolates”), we **cannot distinguish** between these two cases.\n   338\t\n   339\tTherefore, **two draws are not sufficient in worst case**.\n   340\t\n   341\t---\n   342\t\n   343\t### Step 5: Try **three** draws\n   344\t\n   345\tCan we guarantee with **three**?\n   346\t\n   347\tStrategy:\n   348\t\n   349\t1.  411\t\n   412\t### Known result analogy:\n   413\t\n   414\tIn the classic problem with 3 bags (A, O, Mixed), all mislabeled, **1 draw** suffices.\n   415\t\n   416\tHere, with 4 bags and Mixed 590\tHence, the only way to guarantee is to **identify the Mixed bag by drawing a type that cannot be in a pure bag given the label**.\n   591\t\n   592\tThus, the optimal strategy:\n   593\t\n
